planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; trailing New Zealand fuchsia is a coastal groundcover species that tolerates more sun and drier soil than typical upright fuchsias, but still prefers relief from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; trailing New Zealand fuchsia is a coastal groundcover species that tolerates more sun and drier soil than typical upright fuchsias, but still prefers relief from hot afternoon sun. Unlike the pendulous, brightly colored flowers of familiar hybrid fuchsias, this low, wiry-stemmed groundcover produces small, upward-facing flowers with pale yellow-green sepals and no true petals, followed by unusually large, plump, magenta-red berries that are showier than the flowers themselves and edible, if bland. Native to coastal cliffs and rocky ground in New Zealand, it spreads into a dense, trailing mat useful for softening the edge of a raised bed, rock garden, or hanging container in mild-winter climates. It tolerates light frost but is best treated as a container plant brought under cover for winter outside zones 9-10.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bolivian fuchsia is frost-tender and grown as a container specimen brought indoors for winter outside zones 9b-11.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Bolivian fuchsia is frost-tender and grown as a container specimen brought indoors for winter outside zones 9b-11. This large, vigorous, shrubby fuchsia from the Andean cloud forests of Bolivia and Argentina produces long, drooping clusters of slender, tubular, deep red flowers in nearly continuous bloom through the warm season, drawing hummingbirds in large numbers to even a single well-grown plant. Its bold size and shrubby, almost tree-like habit set it apart from the more compact hybrid fuchsias typically grown in hanging baskets, making it a striking specimen for a large container or the back of a shaded border in mild climates. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and feed regularly through the growing season to sustain its heavy, continuous bloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; thyme-leaf fuchsia is a Mexican cloud-forest species that appreciates cooler summer conditions and consistent moisture.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; thyme-leaf fuchsia is a Mexican cloud-forest species that appreciates cooler summer conditions and consistent moisture. Fine, small, thyme-like leaves clothe delicate, arching branches studded nearly year-round with small, slender, pale pink to rose-red flowers, giving the shrub an airy, refined texture distinct from the larger-leaved, gaudier hybrid fuchsias. Native to oak and pine-oak woodlands of Mexico and Central America, it is more heat-tolerant than many species fuchsias while still preferring the dappled shade and humidity of a woodland setting, making it a good choice for a shaded border in warmer climates where typical fuchsias struggle. Pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a bushy habit and continued bloom, and protect from hard freezes in marginal zones.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Congo cockatoo impatiens wants warmth and humidity and sulks in cool or dry conditions.

directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Congo cockatoo impatiens wants warmth and humidity and sulks in cool or dry conditions. Glossy, succulent stems and leaves support unusually shaped, bright golden-yellow flowers marked with a maroon-red blotch and a long, curved nectar spur, giving each bloom a whimsical, bird-like silhouette unlike the flatter faces of familiar bedding impatiens. Native to the forest understory of East Africa, it thrives in warm, humid shade and makes a striking, less-common addition to a tropical-style shade border or large container where its unusual flower form and color can be appreciated up close. Pinch young plants to encourage bushiness, and treat as a tender annual or overwinter cuttings indoors outside zones 10-11.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full shade; trailing plectranthus roots readily from cuttings taken any time during the growing season and spreads quickly in warm, humid shade.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after last frost in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial to full shade; trailing plectranthus roots readily from cuttings taken any time during the growing season and spreads quickly in warm, humid shade. Rounded, scalloped leaves edged in purple and often flushed bronze-purple beneath trail along reddish stems that root as they spread, forming a fast-growing groundcover or cascading container plant topped with airy spikes of small, pale lavender-blue flowers in late summer and fall. Native to forest understories of South Africa, it tolerates deep shade better than most flowering groundcovers and fills bare ground under trees and shrubs quickly, making it useful for covering difficult shaded slopes or spilling from a shaded hanging basket. It is frost-tender and grown as an annual or overwintered from cuttings outside zones 9-11.

planting.note: Sow fine seed on the surface of moist, light, well-drained potting mix in a covered terrarium or humid propagation tray in bright, indirect light; miniature sinningia needs constant humidity and warmth and is grown indoors as a terrarium or windowsill plant rather than outdoors.

directions: Sow fine seed on the surface of moist, light, well-drained potting mix in a covered terrarium or humid propagation tray in bright, indirect light; miniature sinningia needs constant humidity and warmth and is grown indoors as a terrarium or windowsill plant rather than outdoors. One of the smallest members of the gesneriad family, this tiny tuberous perennial forms a rosette barely an inch or two across, covered in soft, dark green, quilted leaves and disproportionately large, tubular violet flowers with a pale throat, blooming almost continuously under good terrarium conditions. Native to the shaded forest floor of Brazil's coastal mountains, it grows from a tiny persistent tuber that can go dormant if conditions turn too dry or cool, resprouting once warmth and humidity return, and self-sows readily inside an enclosed terrarium. Its diminutive scale and constant bloom make it a favorite miniature for gesneriad collectors growing under lights or in bottle gardens rather than a plant for the outdoor garden.
